2339.dq: Más bien, tiene el efecto culminativo de delimitar las palabras dentro de la cadena hablada. Entre los sustantivos y los adjetivos, cada palabra normalmente tiene un solo tono alto, aunque algunas palabras tienen dos.
2339.dloc: Parker 1995, ch. 'La fonología y la ortografía', §4 'El tono', pp. 17-18. Rogers 2021, sec. 2.3 'Stress and tone', pp. 95-97.
2339.prule: Restricted-tone / pitch-accent system (author's classification): each noun or adjective normally carries one high-toned syllable (a few carry two), culminative and word-delimiting; the H rarely falls on the first syllable (except in some disyllables) and every syllable after the H is low; the position of the H/accent is lexically specified and 'mayormente impredecible' (mostly unpredictable), with rare minimal pairs (anáwa 'they' vs anawá 'canoe'). No weight or quantity-insensitive placement rule is given.
2339.srule: Secondary (rhythmic) stresses are predictable although the primary accent is lexical: they fall on alternating syllables counting leftward from the primary accent (the high-toned syllable), i.e. on the even-numbered syllables preceding it ([àpitúri] 'mud; clay', [ràhapúma] 'he or she is blowing', [ramètʸamári] 'he or she is warming it up', [pàriʔàreróti] 'niece', [a:hàbarèʔamáni] 'it is not good'); when the accent lies far enough left a secondary stress may also follow it in the same word (ex. 40); the alternation is quantity-insensitive (long vowels count as a single syllable, exx. 41-42). Not mentioned in Parker 1995 sec. 4 (pp. 17-24); stated by the same author in Parker 1999.

2339.tone: Parker 1995 calls Iñapari 'un idioma tonal restringido' and says 'lo más correcto sería clasificar el iñapari como una lengua de tono-acento (pitch-accent), igual que el nomatsiguenga'; the terms 'acento' and 'tono alto' are used interchangeably ('la ubicación del acento o tono alto'). One H per noun/adjective word (some two: iwáná, aáwíri, itehétíro, ipúʔúri), all post-H syllables low, H rarely initial except in some disyllables; placement mostly unpredictable; rare minimal pairs. All H tones are written with an acute in the vocabulary. The two moras of a long vowel can differ in tone ([mapaá] 'colmena'). §4.1 'Procesos tonales' (pp. 19-24) gives two phrase-level sandhi rules: verb-final L surfaces as H before a following L-initial word; the H on the second syllable of a disyllable delinks after a word ending in H. Rogers 2021 instead calls the culminative prominence 'word stress' (intensity-based, lexically contrastive, overwhelmingly penultimate in his elicited data) and reserves 'tone' for a separate morpheme-bound high pitch. SAPhon codes 'Tone' (from Parker 1999).

tn.translation: Iñapari is a restricted tone language. ... it has the culminative effect of delimiting words within the speech chain. Among nouns and adjectives, each word normally has a single high tone, although some words have two. Except in the case of some disyllabic words, the high tone does not usually fall on the first syllable of the word; this syllable, like all the syllables that follow the high tone, carries a low tone. So the most correct thing would be to classify Iñapari as a pitch-accent (tono-acento) language, like Nomatsiguenga.

2339.cfw: Parker 1995, the dedicated phonological description (his 1999 phonology sketch is also coded as tonal by SAPhon), analyses the single high-pitched syllable per word as restricted tone or pitch accent, while Rogers 2021, from five weeks of fieldwork he calls preliminary, describes the same lexically unpredictable and mostly penultimate prominence as intensity-cued word stress with a separate morpheme-bound high tone, so the two agree on where the prominence falls and differ only on what kind of system it is.

2340.dq: Like some of its neighboring languages, Indus Kohistani has pitch accent, i.e. one high tone per word.
2340.dloc: p. 2, transcription notes directly after the 'Vowels' table and the palatalization paragraph- with p. 3
2340.prule: Lexical, mora-based pitch accent: exactly one high tone per word; on bimoraic nuclei (long vowel, or short vowel + sonorant) the accent surfaces as falling when it sits on the first mora and rising when it sits on the second mora. No positional (syllable-count) rule and no weight rule is stated; the accent is marked lexically on every headword. Second-hand support: Bashir 2004 (reporting Zoller 2005) 'the occurrence of rising or falling pitch is not predictable'; Baart 2003 pp. 9-10 (Shina-type, based on Zoller's then-unpublished work) 'Stress is assigned to one of the moras of the word... underlyingly, only stress is marked, and the relevant domain for stress is the mora'.
2340.quote: Like some of its neighboring languages, Indus Kohistani has pitch accent, i.e. one high tone per word. On long vowels and on short vowels followed by sonorants, the pitch accent is perceived as either rising or falling, depending on whether the accent is on the first or second mora. In this paper I follow Zoller (2005) in that a rising tone is represented with an acute accent as in á and aá, and a falling tone with a grave accent as in à and àa.
2340.loc: p. 2, transcription notes directly after the 'Vowels' table and the palatalization paragraph- with p. 3
2340.idn: Indus Kohistani (ISO 639-3 mvy), the variety spoken in Pattan (river-Indus dialect, not Kandia-Dubair) (a named variety of the language); data: Pattan village near the river Indus, district Kohistan, Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan; oral texts collected 2000-2009 (mainly one female consultant) plus conversations in her…
2340.tone: Lubberger 2016 p. 2 (first-hand, Pattan variety): 'pitch accent, i.e. one high tone per word'; the rising vs falling contrast on long vowels and short-vowel+sonorant nuclei is the accent on the second vs the first mora; notation follows Zoller 2005 (acute = rising, grave = falling). Bashir 2004 review (second-hand report of Zoller 2005 ch. 2, pp. 22-26): 'Zoller finds that Indus Kohistani has a pitch accent system with two pitch accents-one rising and one falling'; 'Present tense forms are always given since the occurrence of rising or falling pitch is not predictable.' Baart 2003 offprint p. 6: Indus Kohistani's tone system 'looks more like that of Shina' ('I base this claim on as yet unpublished work on Indus Kohistani tone by Claus Peter Zoller, corroborated by some preliminary investigations of my own'); pp. 9-10 for Shina-type: 'Stress is assigned to one of the moras of the word' with a rule associating H to the stressed mora, 'underlyingly, only stress is marked, and the relevant domain for stress is the mora'. So: one lexically placed accent per word realised as H on a mora; no source gives a positional stress rule. Rensch/Decker/Hallberg 1992 SSNP1 explicitly excludes phonology (wordlists mark stress with a stroke, no rule).

2343.tone: Ford 1993 treats the whole Kamano-Yate-Yagaria dialect group as 'a lexical tone language' (p.195); his Yate (2 idiolects, Nupagimi) has H and L only, no Extra-high (p.197); ~95% of ~500 disyllables are HL, *HH > HL, no stable/unstable word-final distinction (p.200 item ii); tone sandhi across qualifier+N, NP+NP and N+suffix boundaries operates in Yate as in Move (p.197, p.201). Stress and accent are never mentioned for Yate; the only accent-type remark concerns Move: 'Without this additional tone (which is phonemic), Move would be a pitch-accent or "restricted" tone language' (p.200). Supplementary, for the sister variety Kanite [kani1286] (Gibson & McCarthy treat Inoke as a dialect of Kanite): Young 1962:99 (open, verified) 'In KANITE also, high tone and stress always occur on the same syllable', and the Kanite OPD (data checked 1992) p.3 'Stress occurs on high tone. Kanite has two phonemic tones.'. Those describe Kanite, not Inoke-Yate, and are not transferred to this record; they suggest a tone-bound stress in the group.

2352.prule: Free dynamic word stress: it may fall on any syllable (muşåt final, mére penult, ócniţe antepenult, clópotele pre-antepenult); position is lexically given, mobile within the verb paradigm and contrastive between word forms (adurå 'to bring' vs adúra 'brings'); only content words are stressed, function words are unstressed. No positional or weight rule stated.
2352.srule: Not mentioned in Narumov 2001, §2.1.2 (p. 660; §§2.1.1–2.1.4 read), nor in Hurren 1971, ch. 1 (typescript pp. 35–55): Hurren describes each word-sized 'distributional unit' as a single prominent (stressed) syllable with subsidiary ante- and post-prominent syllables and never discusses secondary prominence.

2353.dq: Because the root syllable is always the stressed syllable in Isu, the suffix vowel is therefore unstressed. (p. 11) -- the statement is framed over the morphological word (root vs prefix/suffix) in citation forms from a 2,246-word lexical database; no phrase-level prominence is discussed.
2353.dloc: sec. 1.13 '"Echo vowels" from imperfective suffixes', p. 11; sec. 1.9 'Unusual retroflexed allophones', p. 8; root/affix templates sec. 1.1-1.2, p. 5; tone sec. 5 / 1.17-1.18, pp. 13-14.
2353.prule: Stress falls on the root syllable, i.e. the first (and normally only full) syllable of the root, template (N1)C1(S1)V1(C2)(V2); the optional final root vowel / imperfective suffix vowel ('echo vowel') is unstressed and reduced (schwa or a weak copy of the root vowel), and the (C)V noun-class prefixes and grammatical markers are outside the root and unstressed. Stress position is thus set by morphological constituency (root vs affix), not by syllable count: a disyllable is prefix+root (stress final) or root+echo vowel (stress initial).
2353.srule: Not mentioned in Anderson 2014 (A phonological sketch of Isu, 18 pp., read in full; stress is mentioned only at sec. 1.9 p. 8 and sec. 1.13 p. 11, both about the root syllable bearing the stress).
2353.quote: When this Isu suffix gets added to roots lacking a C2 consonant, the vowel of the suffix merges with the vowel of the root producing a phonetically long vowel. While this unstressed vowel is often a central schwa, it often takes on the character of the root vowel (thus the “echo vowel” characterization as the suffix vowel sounds like a weak echo of the main root vowel). 2362.dq: Every IM lexical word must have one and only one primary stress [...] Stress is always located within a two syllable window of the right edge of the grammatical word—that is, on the couplet of the word. [p. 90, on enclitics:] Doing so does not change the placement of stress whether the stressed syllable is light, as illustrated in (91), or heavy, as illustrated in (92).

2362.heavy: Heavy = bimoraic syllable: a single vowel node associated with two moras (CVː), including CVˀV (glottal is a laryngeal feature of the vowel, not a coda). End of §3.3 (p. 87): 'The structure represented here constitutes a single heavy (i.e. bimoraic) syllable, whereas the structure in (87) consists of two light (i.e. monomoraic) syllables. There is no other way to form a heavy syllable in IM, a fact that is not surprising given that the language lacks syllable codas, and onsets are not expected to contribute to syllable weight (Hyman 1985).' Heavy syllables occur only as the final syllable of the grammatical word (p. 89).
2362.dflt: penultimate syllable (first syllable of the disyllabic CV.CV couplet); e.g. for 2..8 syllables of all-light words: 10 010 0010 00010 000010 0000010 00000010
2362.prule: One obligatory, culminative primary stress per lexical word, on the initial mora of the word-final couplet (a right-aligned moraic trochee): the final syllable when it is heavy (bimoraic CVː / CVˀV), otherwise the penultimate syllable. Equivalently, stress on the penultimate mora of the grammatical word. Pre-couplet (prefixal) syllables are unfooted and unstressed; postlexical enclitics do not shift stress.
2362.srule: None (tentative): 'I also make the somewhat less emphatic claim that IM does not have secondary stress.' A single foot per prosodic word; pre-foot prefixes and enclitics unfooted. Author leaves open that unreduced compounds could contain two prosodic words and so possibly a secondary stress; no instrumental study.

tn.quote: I propose that, although the IM tone system has three surface tones, the underlying system is best modelled by only two contrastive levels, plus several abstract analytical devices, including floating tones, TBUs unspecified for tone on the surface and tonal coalescence. ... On the first TBU, there is contrast between H and M, and between H and L, but no L ~ M contrast. ... I therefore propose that there is only a two-way contrast on each TBU of the couplet—L and H—and that there is no underlying M level in the tone system.

This reduction in the glides leads to the development of a certain type of rhythm. This occurs in sequences involving glides which are then reduced to a succession of raised highs and highs with a compensatory stress accompanying the raised high tone or the high tone. [p. 33, 3.2]…
2363.prule: Tone language: two basic tones H and L with downstep, upstep and latent low ('see-saw system'), lexically contrastive (minimal pairs to quadruplets). No word-stress or word-accent rule is stated anywhere in Part I Phonology.
2363.srule: Not mentioned in Meier, Meier & Bendor-Samuel 1975, Part I Phonology (chs. 2-6, pp. 29-84): no word stress is posited, hence no secondary stress; the only use of 'stress' is a tempo-dependent compensatory stress on (raised) high tones after glide reduction within the tone span in conversational Register 1 (sec. 3.3.3 p. 34), a phrase-level tonal rhythm, not word stress.
2363.quote: [p. 58, 5.4.1 General features] The tone system is essentially a two tone system with downstep and upstep. It could be called a "see-saw system" more appropriately than a downstep system. Thus the downstepping influence which characterises other Kwa languages and especially Igbo, is counteracted by widely distributed raising influences. The tone system comprises: Two basic tones: High (H or ´), Low (L or `) Three features: Downstep (!) Upstep (^) Latent Low (` before the word) ... Many minimal tone pairs and triplets are found, and some quadruplets: oku eka eba ekwa / HH fire hand vegetable c…
2363.idn: The source describes Izi proper (fieldwork at Abia Unufu, 'the mother village of the Izi', ten miles south of Abakaliki, 1964-71), one member of the Izi-Ezaa-Ikwo(-Mgbo) cluster that Glottolog treats as the language-level language izie1238; Ezaa, Ikwo and Mgbo are not described.
2363.exq_: [p. 36] ... the glide reduction and the devoicing of span final vowels which mark Register 1 are absent from Register 2. [p. 34] The faster the speed of the spans, the more this rhythm develops.
2363.tone: Two-tone (H, L) system with downstep (!), upstep (^) and latent low; raising vs non-raising low variants and a predictable raised-high variant (p. 58). Lexical minimal tone pairs, triplets and quadruplets (oku 'fire/fowl/a bird/heart burn' etc.). The syllable carries only quality (palatalisation/labialisation/neutral) and pitch features (p. 55); the phonological word is delimited only by vowel elision, nasal desyllabification and vowel harmony (p. 46). No word stress or accent is posited. The sole 'stress' remark is a tempo-dependent compensatory stress that rides on (raised) high tones after glide reduction inside the tone span (a unit of one or more phonological words) in Register 1 conversational speech (p. 34); it is absent from Register 2 deliberate speech (p. 36), where the instrumental tracings use a stress symbol '. Stress is thus a by-product of tone realisation in connected fast speech, not a lexical or positional word property.
